name: Armoni
title: Saul's son through Rizpah
summary: Armoni was the son of King Saul and his concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. His fate is inextricably linked to Saul's breach of covenant with the Gibeonites—a crime that, according to the biblical account, brought famine upon Israel during David's reign. When David sought an answer from the Lord, it was revealed that Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites was the cause. The Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants as atonement, and Armoni was handed over along with his brother Mephibosheth (son of Rizpah) and five sons of Merab. They were executed in a ritual act on the hill before the Lord, at the beginning of the harvest. Armoni's mother Rizpah then kept a remarkable and prolonged watch over the dead bodies, protecting them from birds of prey and wild animals. This courageous act moved King David, who had their bones gathered—together with those of Saul and Jonathan—and arranged for an honorable burial in the tomb of Kish in the land of Benjamin. The account raises deep questions about collective guilt, covenant faithfulness, and atonement, and Rizpah's loyalty casts a poignant light on an otherwise brutal episode.

keyEvents.title: Famine in David's time
keyEvents.description: A three-year famine struck Israel, and the Lord revealed that the cause was Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites.

keyEvents.title: The Gibeonites' demand
keyEvents.description: The Gibeonites demanded that seven of Saul's descendants be handed over to them for execution as atonement for Saul's crimes.

keyEvents.title: Handing over and execution
keyEvents.description: Armoni was handed over to the Gibeonites along with his brother Mephibosheth and five sons of Merab. They were executed on a hill in the presence of the Lord at the beginning of the barley harvest.

keyEvents.title: Rizpah's Watch Over the Dead
keyEvents.description: Rizpah spread sackcloth on the rock and kept watch over the bodies from the start of the harvest until rain fell, preventing birds and wild animals from approaching the corpses.

keyEvents.title: David Arranges a Burial
keyEvents.description: When David heard about Rizpah's actions, he retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan as well as those of the executed men and arranged for a dignified burial in the tomb of Kish in the land of Benjamin.

versions.summary: Armoni was one of Saul's sons, born to his concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. He was handed over to the Gibeonites along with his brother Mephibosheth and five other descendants of Saul to atone for Saul's bloodguilt against them. His mother Rizpah kept watch over the dead bodies in a moving act of mourning.
versions.title: Saul's son through Rizpah
versions.reason: [major] There is no biblical evidence that Armoni was a "warrior". He is only known as Saul's son by Rizpah and as one of the seven handed over to the Gibeonites. The role should be changed to something more appropriate, such as 'king's son'.; [minor] The summary is good but should clarify that there were five sons of Merab (not just 'five other descendants of Saul') for clarity. Otherwise, it is theologically correct.; [major] Footnotes are missing. This profile has several interesting historical, theological, and linguistic aspects that should be covered: Rizpah's role, the status of the Gibeonites, and textual critical questions about Merab versus Michal in 2 Sam 21:8.; [minor] In the event 'The Gibeonites' Demand', verse 1 is included even though it was already covered in the previous event. It might be cleaner to start from verse 2.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1. It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from the previous version, and preferably include a bit more context about the theological significance of the event.; [minor] It can be clarified that the execution took place at the beginning of the barley harvest, which provides important context for Rizpah's watch, which lasted from the barley harvest until the rain came.; [minor] The date of death, 1010 BC, is somewhat uncertain. The event occurred during David's reign, traditionally dated to approximately 1010–970 BC. It may be more precise to set the date of death a bit later, for example around 1000 BC, but the uncertainty is great enough that this is acceptable.

versions.summary: Armoni was the son of King Saul and his concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. He is known from the account in 2 Samuel concerning the Gibeonites' revenge. During a prolonged famine in David's reign, it was revealed that Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites was the cause. To atone for this injustice, the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants be handed over. Armoni, his brother Mephibosheth, and five sons of Merab were executed on a hill in a ritual act before the Lord. Afterwards, Rizpah kept a courageous and faithful watch over the dead bodies – an act that deeply moved David and led him to gather their bones and give them a dignified burial in the family tomb in the land of Benjamin.

footnotes.text: The Gibeonites were a Canaanite people who had made a covenant with Israel under Joshua (Josh 9). Saul's attempt to wipe them out broke this covenant and brought bloodguilt upon Israel that needed atonement.

In 2 Sam 21:8, 'five sons of Michal' is mentioned in some Hebrew manuscripts, but the Septuagint and other manuscript traditions read 'Merab.' Since Michal was childless according to 2 Sam 6:23, most textual critics consider 'Merab' to be the original reading.
The name Armoni (Hebrew: אַרְמֹנִי, 'Armoni') may derive from the Hebrew word for 'palace' (אַרְמוֹן, 'armon'), perhaps reflecting his connection to the royal house.

Rizpah's long vigil over the dead bodies (2 Sam 21:10) is one of the most moving scenes about maternal love and loyalty in the Hebrew Bible. Her actions led David to arrange a dignified burial and demonstrate a woman's influence even in a time of limited formal power.

The execution of Saul's descendants raises difficult theological questions about collective guilt and atonement in ancient Israel. The practice of holding descendants accountable for their ancestors' sins was widespread in the ancient Near East but was later criticized by prophets such as Ezekiel (Ezek 18:20), who emphasized individual responsibility.

Ritual execution 'in the presence of the Lord' (2 Sam 21:9) suggests that the act was understood as a sacred action—a form of atonement offering to restore the relationship between God and the people after covenant breach. Such ideas about collective atonement had parallels in other ancient cultures in the region.

Gibeon is identified with modern el-Jib, northwest of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have revealed a significant settlement from the Iron Age, confirming the city's prominent role in the biblical narrative.
